perOption.C: Switching to RDS adds infrastructure management and doesn't necessarily reduce cost for write-heavy workloads.
perOption.D: DynamoDB Streams adds records of all table changes to a stream. This ADDS cost (Streams charges), doesn't reduce WCU usage.

question: A company's ECS service runs on Fargate. They have predictable load during business hours and very low load at night. They want to reduce Fargate costs during off-hours without manual intervention. What should they implement?

options.text: ECS Service Auto Scaling with scheduled scaling actions
Convert the ECS service to EC2 launch type
Reduce Fargate task memory allocation
Enable Fargate Spot for all tasks

explanation.correct: ECS Service Auto Scaling with scheduled scaling: at 6pm, schedule scale task count from 10 to 2. At 7am, schedule scale to 10. Fargate charges per vCPU and memory per second of task runtime. Fewer tasks at night = significantly lower cost.

perOption.A: CORRECT. Scheduled scaling: Application Auto Scaling with scheduled actions. 7am: desired=10, 7pm: desired=2. Predictable pattern → scheduled is more cost-effective than reactive target tracking. Fargate: pay per task second, fewer tasks = lower cost.
perOption.B: EC2 launch type: cluster EC2 instances run even at night (you pay for the nodes). Fargate with fewer tasks at night is cheaper.
perOption.C: Reducing memory allocation saves some cost but doesn't address the fundamental over-provisioning at night.
perOption.D: Fargate Spot: good for interruptible tasks. For predictable business-hours load, scheduled scaling is better because Spot tasks can be interrupted during business hours when you need them most.

question: A company is evaluating whether to migrate from a managed service (ElastiCache Redis managed cluster) to self-managed Redis on EC2. They're trying to reduce costs. What is the PRIMARY cost consideration they are likely missing?

options.text: Self-managed Redis on EC2 requires EC2 Reserved Instances which aren't available
ElastiCache has additional features (automated failover, patching, backups) that require engineering time to replicate on EC2, offsetting compute savings
Self-managed Redis requires more expensive EC2 instance types
ElastiCache pricing per node is always cheaper than equivalent EC2

explanation.correct: ElastiCache (managed) costs more per compute unit than self-managed Redis on EC2. However, ElastiCache includes automated failover, patching, monitoring, backups, and cluster management. Replicating these features on EC2 requires significant engineering time — often more expensive than the pricing delta.

perOption.A: Reserved Instances ARE available for EC2. This is incorrect.
perOption.B: CORRECT. TCO analysis: ElastiCache managed overhead (engineering time) = 0 hrs/week. Self-managed EC2 Redis: setup high availability, automate patching, configure failover, build monitoring, handle incidents. Engineering cost often exceeds compute savings. True for most managed service vs self-managed comparisons.
perOption.C: Self-managed Redis can run on the same or smaller EC2 instance types as ElastiCache uses internally.
perOption.D: ElastiCache pricing is typically HIGHER than equivalent EC2 compute cost (you pay for the management overhead).

question: A company has a large S3 bucket with 5 TB of data. They're receiving unexpectedly high S3 costs. Which TWO factors should they check first?

options.text: Whether GET requests are being made frequently (high request cost)
Whether data is being transferred out to the internet frequently (egress cost)
Whether the bucket is using S3 Standard storage class (should consider cheaper classes)
Whether S3 Versioning is enabled and accumulating old versions
Whether Multi-Part uploads are being used

explanation.correct: S3 egress to internet is $0.09/GB — can quickly add up. Old versions from S3 Versioning accumulate and cost the same as current versions but may be forgotten. Both are common sources of unexpected S3 costs.

perOption.A: GET request costs: S3 charges $0.0004 per 1,000 GET requests. Even billions of requests are a small cost relative to storage and egress.
perOption.B: CORRECT. Data transfer out to internet: $0.09/GB. If an application is serving large files directly from S3 to users globally, egress can cost more than storage. Solution: CloudFront for egress cost reduction.
perOption.C: Storage class is worth checking for optimization but 5 TB of data even in Standard is only ~$115/month. Unexpected HIGH costs usually come from egress or request patterns.
perOption.D: CORRECT. S3 Versioning: enabled bucket keeps every version of every object. If 5 TB bucket has been overwriting objects frequently, actual stored data could be 50+ TB in old versions. Lifecycle rules to expire old versions are critical.
perOption.E: Multipart uploads: incomplete multipart uploads can accumulate storage costs. Less common than versioning but worth checking. Lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after X days.

question: A company wants to prevent their AWS spending from exceeding $5,000/month. If spending reaches $4,500, they want an alert. If spending reaches $5,000, they want to automatically apply an SCP to restrict new resource creation. Which service enables automated action on budget breach?

options.text: AWS Cost Explorer with email alerts
AWS Budgets with Budget Actions
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
AWS Trusted Advisor cost alerts

explanation.correct: AWS Budgets with Budget Actions: create a cost budget with $4,500 alert threshold (SNS/email) and $5,000 action threshold (apply SCP or IAM policy automatically). Budget Actions can automatically apply SCPs or IAM policies when thresholds are breached.

perOption.A: Cost Explorer has alerts but doesn't have automated actions (SCP application).
perOption.B: CORRECT. AWS Budgets: alert at $4,500 → SNS notification. Action at $5,000 → automatically apply SCP to restrict resource creation. Budget Actions support: apply SCP, apply IAM policy, target EC2/RDS instances. Fully automated enforcement.
perOption.C: Cost Anomaly Detection identifies unusual spending but doesn't have automated enforcement actions.
perOption.D: Trusted Advisor cost alerts are basic recommendations. No automated enforcement actions.

question: A startup uses Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling for their web application. They've grown and now want to reduce compute costs by 60% while maintaining the same availability. The workload is stateless and fault-tolerant. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Purchase 3-year Reserved Instances for all instances
Use a mixed instances policy in the ASG with 70% Spot and 30% On-Demand
Reduce the number of running instances by half
Switch to smaller instance types

explanation.correct: Mixed instances policy: 30% On-Demand (baseline availability, no interruption risk) + 70% Spot (up to 90% discount). Multiple Spot instance pools (different types/AZs) reduce interruption probability. Stateless fault-tolerant workloads are ideal for Spot. 70% Spot × 90% savings ≈ 63% overall savings.

perOption.A: 3-year RI: up to 72% savings. But requires 3-year commitment for a startup. Less flexible. Can't reduce the instance count easily.
perOption.B: CORRECT. Mixed instances policy: On-Demand base (30%) + Spot fleet (70%). Multiple Spot pools (c5.large, m5.large, r5.large in 3 AZs) for diversity. Fault tolerant workload → Spot interruptions handled by ASG (replaces interrupted Spot with new Spot or On-Demand). ~60% overall savings.
perOption.C: Reducing instances halves capacity, which degrades availability. Not a valid solution.
perOption.D: Smaller instances reduce cost but also capacity. Doesn't achieve 60% cost reduction while maintaining same availability.

question: A company uses Amazon Route 53 for DNS. They have resources in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. They notice they're being charged for cross-Region DNS queries. How can they reduce Route 53 DNS query costs?

options.text: Enable Route 53 Resolver query logging
Reduce DNS TTL to 60 seconds to improve freshness
Increase DNS TTL to reduce query frequency
Switch to AWS Global Accelerator instead of Route 53

explanation.correct: DNS TTL (Time-to-Live) controls how long DNS resolvers cache the response. Higher TTL = fewer DNS queries (cached longer) = lower Route 53 query costs. Trade-off: longer TTL means slower propagation when records change.

perOption.A: Query logging adds cost (stores logs in CloudWatch/S3). Doesn't reduce query volume.
perOption.B: Lower TTL (60s): DNS cache expires every 60 seconds → more frequent queries → higher Route 53 costs. Opposite of the goal.
perOption.C: CORRECT. Higher TTL (e.g., 300-3600s): resolvers cache DNS responses longer. Clients use cached response → fewer Route 53 queries → lower query costs. Note: Route 53 charges $0.40/million queries. Cost reduction depends on query volume.
perOption.D: Global Accelerator provides static IPs and routes to the nearest endpoint. Doesn't replace DNS for all use cases and isn't primarily a cost optimization tool.
